title: Family Connections: An Examination of Intrapersonal and Social-Relational Outcomes.
abstract: Family members and other loved ones supporting individuals with borderline personality disorder (BPD) frequently experience elevated burden, depression, and psychological distress, highlighting the need for interventions that directly address their well-being. Interventions that target the social-emotional context of those with BPD have the potential for not only reducing distress in this group but also positively impacting their symptoms and functioning. The present study examined the effectiveness of Family Connections (FC), a peer-led, psychoeducational and skills-training program for family members, friends, and romantic partners of people with BPD, as well as whether change in coping skills mediated the change in outcome variables. A national sample of Canadian participants (n = 101) completed questionnaires before and after a 12-week FC group. Repeated-measures ANOVAs supported significant changes in caregiver burden, F(1, 78) = 13.66, p < 0.001, emotion regulation, F(1, 78) = 18.55, p < 0.001, hope, F(1, 78) = 16.25, p < 0.001, and both functional, F(1, 78) = 28.34, p < 0.001, and dysfunctional coping skills use, F(1, 78) = 29.45, p < 0.001. Significant gains were observed for belongingness, F(1, 78) = 7.66, p < 0.01. No significant changes were found in depression, anxiety, stress, shame, or interpersonal functioning. Mediation analyses did not support functional or dysfunctional coping as mechanisms of change. Overall, findings provide evidence for FC's effectiveness in improving well-being among group participants. Results underscore the importance of accessible, skills-based supports for families navigating chronic emotion dysregulation and suicidality while also identifying domains that may require more intensive or targeted intervention in future research.
